prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which opened the 10^-18 regime of frequency metrology

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on one clean, original idea, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift of the clock transition cancels, and on a decisive realisation that took strontium clocks to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. That is a new regime of what can be measured and how accurately. It is already in use for tests of fundamental constants, searches for dark-sector physics and relativistic geodesy, and it is the leading route to a redefinition of the second. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) reproduce and surpass the original benchmarks, so the physics is stable rather than provisional. The credit is concentrated: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier. That makes a two-person prize without the truncation problems of most other shortlisted entries. On reading the other ballots, B002 is the only candidate with support from at least five members, and it is ranked by members whose own fields are far from precision atomic physics (Pearce, Olsson), which gives me some comfort that this is not only a view from my corner.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is cumulative recognition: the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control) cover the frequency-comb and single-ion foundations, and a skeptical colleague can read lattice clocks as an excellent refinement of an already honoured line rather than a new discovery. A second reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest practical payoff is still prospective. Third, credit beyond the two names (Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Derevianko on theory, and the earlier lattice trapping ideas) is not fully resolved by the supplied credit set.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the experimental Higgs discovery (B053) first and ranks the lattice clock only eighth, partly because the 2005 and 2012 prizes could reduce appetite for a further metrology award.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously, but I do not think it is decisive. The comb and the ion-control prizes recognised enabling tools and a different system; neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping is a distinct conceptual step, and it is what allowed 1e-18 stability through large atom numbers. On B053 I agree the discovery is exceptional and the 2013 prize left the experimental side unrewarded. My difficulty is attribution: Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee are founders and spokespersons, not discoverers, and several of you, Lindroth and Johansson among them, say the same. I would rather not build the prize on a proxy for thousands of people when a cleanly attributed candidate exists. If the committee accepts that proxy, B053 is a serious alternative, not one I would oppose on science.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B038) first as an original, clearly posed theory-plus-experiment story that opened a new field, and acknowledges that timing is a judgment call.
responses.response: I agree the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the Jarillo-Herrero experiments is the cleanest theory-plus-experiment story on the list, and I ranked it fourth for that reason. My disagreement is about maturity. Both you and Johansson list the superconducting mechanism as unresolved, and the discovery is eight years old. Lattice clocks have two decades of independent confirmation and a stable interpretation, so I would not trade a settled achievement for a field whose central question is still open. The experimental credit also reaches Cao and others who are outside a three-name set, which is a fairness problem a clock prize does not have.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B017) first as the architecture behind essentially every superconducting quantum processor, while noting that the 2025 prize in superconducting circuits and the Girvin versus Blais choice complicate it.
responses.response: Circuit QED is a major light-matter achievement and I do not dispute its impact. I see two obstacles that you partly name yourself: a four-name credit set squeezed into three seats with Blais as the loser, and the closeness to the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize. Awarding a closely adjacent platform one year later seems to me harder to defend than a prize in a different area of atomic physics. I also think the two clock ballots and your fifth-place ranking show we are not far apart on B002, where the attribution question does not arise.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and trapped-ion quantum computing (B033) second, but warns that Wineland and Monroe are missing from the credited names and that the 2012 and 2022 prizes make novelty a question.
responses.response: We agree on the top choice and our second choices coincide, which should be treated as one view held twice, since we are both from atomic and optical physics. Your point that the experimental credit in B033 is incomplete without Wineland or Monroe is the main reason I keep it as an alternative and not as a co-equal part of the prize. I would add that the overlap with the 2012 prize is stronger for B033 than for the clocks, because the Wineland-group ion-gate work sits directly beneath it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 and 2012 prizes as making a lattice-clock prize cumulative, or as the foundation that makes it timely.
Whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited, or whether the demonstrated 1e-18 performance is already sufficient.

Whether theory (for example Derevianko) or other early lattice-clock groups such as Takamoto and Lemonde should displace or join the two credited names; I have not verified priority details beyond my recollection.
How heavily the committee will weigh the attribution problem in the Higgs and EHT entries against the maturity concerns of the moire entry.
statement.conflict_note: A possible perceived connection: my profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is associated with Hall's group and JILA. I do not regard this as a decisive conflict, but it should be on the record and the committee may wish to consider whether I should abstain on B002. I also have no documented relationship with Katori. My own work (rare-earth-ion crystals and quantum memories, in Lund) does not overlap with lattice clocks, and none of my listed Lund colleagues appears in the shortlisted credited names.
